claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase and compositionally complex.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
Sustained high-temperature cyclic loading causes stress-assisted, thermally activated segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation triggers the formation of nanoscale intergranular phases.
The nanoscale intergranular phases are intrinsically brittle.
High temperature and cyclic stress locally enhance atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility permits local compositional deviations from the high-entropy equilibrium at grain boundaries.
Local compositional deviations reduce the effective configurational entropy at grain boundaries.
Reduced effective configurational entropy facilitates local ordering and phase separation.
Local ordering and phase separation lead to nucleation of brittle grain-boundary precipitates.
High-temperature cyclic loading will produce greater measurable grain-boundary segregation than room-temperature cyclic loading or high-temperature static loading.
High-temperature cyclic loading will produce nanoscale brittle precipitates relative to the controls.
High-temperature cyclic loading will reduce fracture toughness relative to the controls.
Samples maintained at room temperature retain the original homogeneous microstructure and toughness.
Samples held at high temperature without cyclic loading retain the original homogeneous microstructure and toughness.
The proposed degradation mechanism operates only when both temperature and cyclic-loading amplitude exceed critical thresholds.
Below the critical temperature or loading threshold, significant intergranular segregation and toughness degradation will not occur.
An experiment near 700°C comparing cyclic loading with room-temperature cyclic loading and 700°C static loading can test the hypothesis.
